public.problem: You give customers store credit for free, or you tried in-person selling once, and months later you find hundreds of dollars on your bill for money you never collected. ideas.problemStatement: An owner who gave store credit away free was 'charged $546.10 in fees from June to November on money I never collected', plus about $290 for POS Pro on a store with no POS sales, and Shopify 'refused any refund or even a partial goodwill credit'. The rule is published (stores created on or after 12 May 2025 pay third-party transaction fees on store-credit and gift-card payments), but the admin shows no warning, and POS Pro refunds close 7 days after a monthly billing date. Other owners report charges after uninstalling apps; those are usually final charges for time used, and some were refunded.
ideas.description: The owner installs it from the Shopify App Store and drops in the bill CSV from Settings > Billing; it reads orders, payment methods and POS locations through the Admin API, or from the orders CSV for older months. It leads with two leaks no other app checks: third-party transaction fees on store-credit and gift-card payments (only stores created on or after 12 May 2025 pay them), and POS Pro billed on locations with no POS sales. Each flag shows the amount to date, the fix where one exists (single-use 100% discount codes instead of store credit given away free, confirmed with a free test order; downgrading an idle location to the free POS level), the plain cost where no cheaper setting exists (gift cards sold for money), and the refund deadline where Shopify publishes one (POS Pro: 7 days after a monthly billing date, 30 days after an annual one). App charges after an uninstall and annual renewals are shown as a calendar, without claiming a fix. A daily job watches new store-credit and gift-card payments and idle locations, and a bill-day email asks for the new bill.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners of small Shopify shops (1 to 10 people) on Basic or Grow whose store was created on or after 12 May 2025 and that give store credit (loyalty, refunds as credit, free-credit programmes) or sell gift cards, or that pay for POS Pro on a location; older stores never pay the store-credit or gift-card fee.
ideas.buyer: The shop owner, on the business card, from the same budget as the shop's apps.
ideas.whyNow: Stores created on or after 12 May 2025 pay third-party transaction fees on store-credit and gift-card payments, while a 2024 community answer still says store credit carries no fee, so every store opened in the last 18 months is exposed to advice that is wrong for it. POS Pro refunds close 7 days after a monthly billing date. Three bill or app-spend apps launched between November 2025 and August 2026 with 0 reviews, four similar fee or invoice audit listings now read 'not currently available', and none looks at fees or POS Pro.

mvpScope.buildEstimate: 6 build days, plus Shopify App Store review time, which is outside the build, plus a Level 1 protected-customer-data review.

ideas.techStack: React + Vite static front end; Shopify embedded app shell (App Bridge, OAuth, session tokens) and webhooks on backend-hub (Render); Shopify Admin GraphQL API (read_orders, read_locations) and Shopify Billing API; shared Supabase project for per-shop data; platform scheduled job and transactional email.

pricing.model: Per-shop annual subscription; first bill check free
pricing.rationale: A monthly plan invites cancelling after the one-time fix (switching to discount codes, downgrading POS Pro); the month-to-month app diff is already in AppTrim Unlimited at $15/month. On Basic the store-credit fee passes $49 a year only above about $2,450 a year of redeemed credit.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 120 shops x $49/year = about $5,900 a year (about $490 MRR) after 12 months, assuming App Store search brings about 40 installs a month and a quarter of installs find a leak and pay. AppTrim and Watchdog show 0 reviews after 5 to 12 months, so the low case is close to zero.
ideas.distribution: Shopify App Store listing, a self-serve channel; AppTrim shows that an app built on bill uploads is accepted there. A free public fee calculator page for search traffic on store-credit fee and POS Pro refund queries. Shopify Community: its FAQ allows promoting an app only on the Ask and Offer board ('App recommendations are allowed only on the Ask and Offer board.'), with disclosure of 'any ownership, employment, affiliate, or other commercial relationship' (https://community.shopify.com/faq); its rule on market research or survey posts: rule unknown: check before posting.

validationTest.method: A one-page leak calculator outside the App Store. The owner enters the plan, the month the store opened, store credit and gift cards redeemed per month, POS locations and their POS sales; the page shows the yearly avoidable fees and the cheaper settings, then a 'Watch my bills: $49 a year, refundable pre-order' button and an optional 'What happened to you?' comment box. Traffic comes from a small search-ad test on queries such as 'shopify store credit transaction fee', 'shopify POS Pro refund' and 'shopify charged after uninstalling app'. No outreach: nobody in the evidence is contacted and nothing is posted in the evidence threads.
validationTest.successCriteria: In three weeks: at least 400 visitors, 40 calculator runs at under $5 each, a quarter of runs showing a leak over $100 a year, and 4 refundable pre-orders or 12 price-button clicks, and at least 3 visitors describe a leak of their own in the comment box.
validationTest.cost: One build day for the page, $200 in search ads, three weeks of waiting.

ideas.moat: Thin. The rules (the fee cut-off date, plan rates, POS Pro windows, app billing cycles) are public. The defensible parts are a parser tested on real bill exports, a rule set kept current as Shopify changes fees, and each shop's saved bill history. Shopify could add a native warning at any time.
compliance: GDPR and UK GDPR: holds owners' contact data and bill line items; orders are read for payment method, amount and location only; public apps must answer Shopify's mandatory privacy webhooks.
Shopify App Store requirements: Shopify Billing for the app's own charges (1.2.1), only necessary scopes with read_all_orders justified (3.2, 3.2.1), expiring offline tokens (3.1.2).
No financial advice: figures are estimates from Shopify's published rates, and refunds stay Shopify's or the developer's decision.
Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA for the embedded page and the upload page.

Protected customer data: orders and transactions are Level 1 protected customer data (no name, address, phone or email fields), which a public app must request and pass review for, with data minimisation, merchant data-protection agreements, retention periods and encryption at rest and in transit (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/protected-customer-data.md).

scoreRationale.pain: One recent merchant complaint hits the job (https://community.shopify.com/t/722775.json, 2026-11-25); the others are app charges after uninstalling, one refunded in full (https://apps.shopify.com/reviews/2385947), and two community searches since 2026-05-31 found no other store-credit or POS Pro complaint: 3.
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: Paid apps exist for the app-charge part only (https://apps.shopify.com/apptrim at $9 per invoice or $15/month; https://apps.shopify.com/app-cost-audit-monitor at $9.99/month), and none shows a buyer: 0 reviews.
scoreRationale.reachability: Self-serve channel only: the Shopify App Store, where the upload-based AppTrim lists (https://apps.shopify.com/apptrim) but has 0 reviews a year after launch; the Community allows promotion only on Ask and Offer (https://community.shopify.com/faq).
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Re-scoped to fees on store credit and gift cards, idle POS Pro and refund windows, no listing covers them (https://apps.shopify.com/apptrim, https://apps.shopify.com/app-cost-audit-monitor) and Shopify only discloses the rule (https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/customers/store-credit); not 5, because Shopify could add a warning and the app-charge part is free or native (https://shopify.dev/changelog/posts/shopify-app-pricing-charge-for-usage-recurring-subscriptions-or-both.md).
scoreRationale.feasibility: Rules on uploaded CSVs fit the platform in days, but bills cannot be read by API (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/billing), the bill CSV is undocumented, POS Pro status is not in the API (https://community.shopify.dev/t/easy-way-to-identify-pos-pro-locations-via-graphql-api/21289), and listing needs OAuth, App Bridge and Shopify Billing (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/shopify-app-store/app-store-requirements).
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: No sector regulation, but orders and transactions are Level 1 protected customer data needing Shopify's review, a merchant data agreement, retention periods and encryption (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/protected-customer-data.md): 4.

review.findings: The reviewer re-read the founding complaint and found that it is the only recent complaint about fees on store credit or gift cards or idle POS Pro; two more community searches (third-party transaction fees; POS Pro subscription, both since 2026-05-31) found no other, and the remaining complaints concern plan charges on stores the app would never be installed on, an app developer's refund policy, or a final charge refunded in full, so pain falls from 4 to 3 and those items were dropped from the evidence. Shopify's fees and store-credit help pages confirm the rule for stores created on or after 12 May 2025, with no 2026 change and no admin warning described, and the Fall '26 Edition adds none. The app-charge part is already free or native (AppTrim's free invoice, Watchdog's free plan, Shopify's App Pricing billing card since May 2026), and four similar fee or invoice audit listings now read 'not currently available'. The idea was re-scoped to lead with fees and idle POS Pro, competitiveGap rises from 3 to 4, and the total stays at 20, provisional. The reviewer also corrected the compliance text (orders are Level 1 protected customer data needing Shopify review), moved pricing to annual only because the main fixes are one-time, and noted that gift cards sold for money have no cheaper setting.

public.problem: You open your Thanksgiving or Christmas menu on Square and most customers check out with the first pickup time they are offered, so you spend the week calling them to confirm the real day. You set up the dates item by item, and changing your pickup hours for one week means changing them back by hand afterwards. Then you count how many pies to bake for each day by going through the orders one at a time.

benefits: Every order arrives with the pickup day the customer actually chose
Set up a whole holiday menu once, with its own pickup days and order deadline
No more orders on any one day than you can make
A prep list for each pickup day, ready to print
Reuse this year's menu next year

ideas.problemStatement: Food sellers on Square open a holiday menu and customers check out with the earliest pickup slot Square assigns, so one seller confirms about 70% of Thanksgiving orders by hand. Pre-order rules are set item by item, a pre-order window can make the whole store say it is not accepting orders, one seller's Sunday-only pre-order day still offers Saturday pickup (possibly a settings issue), and there is no way to change pickup hours for one week and have them revert (a Square Champion: the feature does not exist yet). And Square gives no item totals per pickup day (a free early-access tool, CafeKit, exists only to fill that).
ideas.description: A pre-order page the seller links from their site or social posts. The owner connects Square, builds a holiday or weekly menu from their Square items, and sets pickup days, windows, a cut-off and a cap per day; that menu's hours never touch the store's regular Square hours. Customers pick a pickup day first, see only what is available that day, and pay through the seller's own Square account. Each order is written into Square as a paid pickup order with the chosen time and a prep-time offset, so it shows in Order Manager and reaches kitchen printers and the kitchen display at pickup time minus the prep time set on the menu. The app closes the menu at the cut-off or when a day is full and emails the next day's prep list. It is for sellers who want pre-orders kept in Square rather than in a separate storefront such as Hotplate or Homegrown.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners and managers of one- to three-location bakeries, pie shops, caterers, butchers and coffee shops in the US that sell through Square (Square Online, the online ordering profile or Square for Restaurants) and take pickup pre-orders for holidays or weekly bake days, and who want pre-orders to stay inside Square (one catalog, one payout, orders in Order Manager and on kitchen printers) rather than in a separate pre-order storefront.
ideas.buyer: The owner, on the business card. No seller in the evidence is shown paying for a pre-order add-on; category prices are Homegrown at $10 a month and Hotplate's per-order fee, which sellers can pass to customers. Square Online preorders need Plus ($49 a month per location) or Premium, but item pre-ordering on online ordering profiles names no plan.
ideas.whyNow: The Thanksgiving complaints were posted between 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-19, and the Christmas, Valentine's Day, Lunar New Year and Easter pre-order seasons follow; a Square Champion confirmed on 2026-11-10 that one-week pickup-hour overrides do not exist; an archived 2020 Square request for date and time selection on pre-orders drew 333 replies, and the same questions came back in 2022, 2023, 2025 and 2026, so the gap has outlasted six seasons. Square shipped item-level pre-ordering for ordering profiles (2026-04-23, 2026-06-04) and pre-orders for sold-out items (2026-09-24), but its 2026-10-22, 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-19 'What's New From Square' posts announce no pickup-day-first rule, menu-level setup or per-day cap.

ideas.problemStatement: Closing the cash drawer on Square "live[s] in our heads or on paper": the closer counts on a sheet or a phone app, types one total into Square, and nobody can tell later "who added this wrong". Square records starting and expected cash, emails a cash report and can hide the expected figure from staff, and free phone counters handle bills and coins, but nothing links the count to Square's expected cash for each drawer session or keeps a history by register and by who was on the drawer. So some owners stopped having staff count at all, and others rebuild it in their own spreadsheets.
ideas.description: A closer opens the count screen on the register tablet or a phone, enters a 4-digit PIN, picks the register and counts bills and coins by denomination; the screen never receives an expected figure. The app then says which bills and coins to leave as tomorrow's float and what goes in the deposit bag. The closer still taps End Drawer in Square POS, because Square's API cannot record a count. A backend job uses a read-only Square connection: it lists the location's drawer sessions, retrieves each one for its expected cash, paid in and out, device name and the team members logged in during it, matches the session to the count through the register-to-device map the owner set up, and records the variance. The owner sees variance per drawer session with its closer and everyone else on that drawer, trends by register and staff over weeks, and a CSV export, which Square's Dashboard cannot produce. A nightly email flags sessions outside tolerance and repeat shortfalls on the same register or staff roster.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners and shift managers at cash-heavy Square counters with 1 to 7 registers that run Square Cash Management on an iPad, Android tablet, Square Terminal, Register or Handheld: cafés, pubs, counter-service restaurants and small grocers, and food trucks or market stalls only when they use one of those devices, not a phone. Closers use the count screen nightly.

ideas.whyNow: The 2026-09-22 cash-close request is the top-kudos Square idea since May, and a second request followed on 2026-11-18. Sellers arriving from Toast, Redtail and grocery POS systems lose a close they had, and Square's release notes from 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-19 have no cash-drawer item. Its API is open while the App Marketplace is paused. Tillwise launched a paid blind close for Shopify POS on 2026-09-16, with per-staff variance in its $29 Pro plan, which shows a vendor expects this to pay on another POS, though it had no reviews on 2026-11-27.

scoreRationale.reachability: App Marketplace onboarding is paused (https://developer.squareup.com/forums/t/listing-square-apps-marketplace/28043) and the Community forbids unprompted promotion (https://community.squareup.com/t5/Community-Resources/Square-Community-Code-of-Conduct/ta-p/723469); the only channel left is search with a free counter page and ads.
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Free tools cover most of the job: Square hides the expected amount through the one customizable permission set every account has (https://squareup.com/help/us/en/article/5822-employee-permissions), a free phone app counts by denomination with float and deposit totals (https://apps.apple.com/app/id1397689734), and two developers are pitching Square-connected tools in https://community.squareup.com/t5/Feature-Requests/Redesign-the-end-of-day-cash-closing-flow-denomination-counting/idi-p/849765; only the count matched to Square's expected cash, and its history, is unserved: 2.
scoreRationale.feasibility: The read-only Cash Drawer Shifts API gives expected cash, paid in and out, device and closing team member per shift (https://developer.squareup.com/reference/square/objects/CashDrawerShift, https://developer.squareup.com/docs/cashdrawershift-api/reporting); about 6 days on the platform, with matching and the phone exclusion as the hard parts.
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Light but present: per-closer records about named staff from team_member_ids (https://developer.squareup.com/reference/square/objects/CashDrawerShift) plus custody of a Square token, which a seller in https://community.squareup.com/t5/Feature-Requests/Redesign-the-end-of-day-cash-closing-flow-denomination-counting/idi-p/849765 refused to share.

review.findings: The reviewer rechecked both threads through the community API by rank and author ID, recording none: 849765 has nine distinct authors, three of them developers or vendors, and 853008 has four, with no shared author, so the two evidence items stand as independent and recent. Square's release notes from 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-19 add nothing on cash drawers, and every Square account has one customizable permission set, so hiding the expected amount is free. A free iPhone register-and-safe counter with a deposit total, and a phone app one Square seller's staff use, already cover the denomination count and much of the float and deposit split. The only priced tool for the exact job, on Shopify POS, still has 0 reviews ten weeks after launch, while the Square sellers in the evidence use sheets or free apps, or stopped counting, and one says they should not have to rely on third-party apps; so competitiveGap falls from 3 to 2 and willingnessToPay from 3 to 2, for a total of 19. The idea is re-scoped to what nothing free does: each count matched to Square's expected cash per drawer session, with history by register and roster, export and a nightly digest; the read-only API supports this, but Square lists everyone logged in during a session, so the app must not pin a shared-drawer shortfall on the closer. The draft's ad test, which could not reach its visitor target on its budget, was replaced by a 21-day test with a refundable founding payment.

ideas.problemStatement: Restaurant hours change every week and around every holiday, and each change has to be made separately in each place that shows them: 'lots of work every week, can we have them all sync to be the same?' Owners commissioning new websites ask that 'restaurant staff should be able to update prices, change holiday hours, and add specials without hiring a developer', with the menu on the page rather than in a PDF. None of the complaints found names the website or Google: they name Square's ordering channels and the delivery apps.
ideas.description: Staff keep one menu and a list of dated specials, with holiday dates, in a simple editor. A small embed shows the menu and today's specials on the restaurant's own website as accessible HTML. With the owner's permission the app writes the same menu to the Google Business Profile's food menu and the holiday dates to its special hours, after showing what will change; Google shows special hours only on the dates set, so nothing there has to be changed back. A scheduled job starts and ends specials on their dates and emails a change-day and change-back checklist for channels with no API, such as Square Online pickup hours and delivery apps. It is aimed at sites that do not already get this free: not WordPress sites, where a free plugin copies regular and special hours from Google, and not Toast sites, whose menus already sync to Google. Every change goes into a log with who made it and when.

mvpScope.buildEstimate: About 6 build days on the platform, but only after Basic API Access is approved and OAuth works for a non-test account; 2026 developer reports show both stalling for weeks with no reply.

ideas.techStack: Static React + Vite front end on the HintWise platform; the shared Supabase project for sign-in and per-app tables (locations, menu items, specials, hours, overrides, change log); backend-hub on Render for Google OAuth tokens, the Business Profile API calls and the scheduled job; transactional email for reminders; a small JavaScript embed that renders server-generated accessible HTML.

pricing.pricePoint: $24/month for one location; $59/month for 2 to 5 locations
pricing.rationale: About a quarter of Marqii's $90 per location on an annual contract and under GBPPromote's $57 for Google alone, while covering the website menu too; above the $5 Wix app, which does not handle holiday hours or menus. Moz Local lists from $16 per location per month on annual billing (2024 comparison page), so $24 is not the cheapest listings option; the case rests on the website menu and specials being included.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 60 single-location restaurants x $24 + 10 groups x $59 = $1,440 + $590 = about $2,030 MRR after 12 months, assuming roughly 2% of plugin installs and ad visitors convert.
ideas.distribution: Self-serve only; the owner's network does not reach restaurants. (1) WordPress plugin directory: a free, accessible restaurant menu-and-specials block, not an hours block: the free Opening Hours plugin (5,000+ installs) already copies hours from Google, and a WordPress-to-Google-profile sync plugin closed permanently on 2026-06-13 with no reviews. Rule: Guideline 6, 'Plugins that act as an interface to some external third party service (e.g. a video hosting site) are allowed', and Guideline 5, 'Plugins may not contain functionality that is restricted or locked, only to be made available by payment or upgrade' (https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/wordpress-org/detailed-plugin-guidelines/). (2) A small search-ad test on queries about changing holiday hours on the website and the listing together: rule unknown: check before running. (3) Later, a Square App Marketplace listing that imports the menu from a seller's Square catalogue: search results describe an App Partner application and a QA review, but its docs pages returned 404 to this run, so rule unknown: check before listing. (4) Square Seller Community: rule unknown: check before posting; never post in the threads cited as evidence.

validationTest.method: No outreach. (1) For four weeks from 2026-11-30, through Christmas and New Year, a weekly passive count of new owner posts (not developers, agencies or vendors; check who wrote each) in the Square Seller Community and the Google Business Profile Help Community saying that holiday or special hours, specials or the menu were wrong on Google or the website, or had to be entered in both. (2) A landing page leading with one menu and dated specials published to the website and Google's food menu, plus holiday hours, with a waitlist, a price button at $24 a month and one optional question, 'Where do you change your hours and menu today?', fed by a $150 two-week search-ad test on queries about updating the menu or holiday hours on Google and the website together (ad rules: check before running). Contacts nobody and posts in no thread.
validationTest.successCriteria: At least 3 independent owner complaints naming Google or the website in the four weeks; and in two weeks at least 400 visitors, 20 waitlist sign-ups and 6 price-button clicks, with at least half of the answers naming Google or the website.
validationTest.cost: About 4 hours to build the page, $150 in ads, and 30 minutes a week for the count.

ideas.moat: Thin. It rests on the saved menu, holiday calendar and change history for each restaurant, on approved Google API access (a 60-day verified profile and a review), and on plugin installs. Marqii or GBPPromote could cut prices or add month-to-month terms.
compliance: Accessibility: the website menu embed must meet WCAG 2.2 AA (headings, lists, prices as text, no PDF), because restaurant websites are public-facing; this is also a selling point.

Google API terms: access needs an approved Basic API Access application, and every write uses the owner's OAuth grant with business.manage. Google's console lists that scope as non-sensitive, but developers report in 2026 that non-test users get '403 access_denied ... developer-approved testers' and no verification path is offered (https://discuss.google.dev/t/oauth-business-manage-shown-as-non-sensitive-in-auth-platform-but-backend-blocks-all-external-users-with-error-403-access-denied-no-submit-for-verification-path-exists/384175).
Data: business data and staff sign-in emails only; no consumer, student or payment data; GDPR is minimal, limited to staff accounts outside the US.
Menu accuracy: prices and dietary labels are the restaurant's statements; the change log records who published them.

review.findings: The reviewer re-read the two November Square threads and found that neither mentions Google or the website; the only Square request for Google special-hours sync dates from 2024-03-07, so pain drops from 4 to 3. The three freelance jobs are one-off website builds and a local-SEO retainer, not recurring menu and hours updates, so willingnessToPay rests on listing tools alone (Marqii $90, GBPPromote $57, Moz Local from $16 per location on a 2024 comparison page) and drops from 4 to 3, and the SEO retainer was removed from the evidence. Google's food-menu API is current (dietary options added 2026-10-09), but 2026 developer threads report Basic API Access stuck at 0 requests per minute for weeks and external OAuth users blocked with no verification path, so feasibility drops from 3 to 2. The new total is 17 (pain 3, willingnessToPay 3, reachability 3, competitiveGap 1, feasibility 2, complianceBurden 5); the idea misses the gate on total and pain and ships only as provisional.

gateGap.closedBy: The landing-page test goes at the largest gap, the total (15 of 22), through its weakest parts: eight or more waitlist sign-ups from developers whose booking code is in their own repository would show the pain is felt (pain 3), and three or more paid pre-orders at $19 or more, with the free Screen Reader Journeys engine named on the page, would raise willingnessToPay to 4, for a total of 17. Validated also needs pain 4 (recent complaints from booking-page developers or their clients, not agent-written gates), a gap beyond the engine's own free workflows (competitiveGap) and a channel that brings buyers (reachability).

notes.stateful: Each booking flow keeps its saved journey (the labels of its service, staff, time, details and confirm steps) and a dated history of transcripts the developer comes back to.

notes.unattended: The Action runs on every pull request, and a weekly hosted re-run emails the developer when what is announced changes.

ideas.summary: For freelance developers and small agencies who build booking pages for salons, barbers, clinics and garages: runs the booking journey the way a screen-reader user would, records what is heard and where focus goes, flags the usual booking faults, and makes a dated page to hand to the client.

public.summary: Runs your booking page the way a blind customer would, records what their screen reader says at each step, and gives you a page you can hand to your client.
public.problem: You build a booking page for a salon or a clinic, and the automatic accessibility checks all pass. But nobody has listened to what a screen reader says when a customer picks a time or makes a mistake, so you cannot say whether a blind customer can finish a booking. Your client may be the one who finds out, from an unhappy customer or a demand letter.
public.forWhom: Freelance developers and small agencies who build or customise online booking for salons, barbers, clinics, garages and studios.
benefits: Know a screen-reader user can finish a booking before you ship
Catch the usual booking slips: a chosen time never announced, focus lost after each step, errors nobody hears
Hand your client a dated record of what was heard
Re-check automatically every time the booking page changes

ideas.problemStatement: Teams building appointment and booking screens pass their automated checks but cannot say what a screen reader actually announces: 'No spoken screen-reader output was captured' (a counselling platform's appointment calendar, 2026-11-19, where the fault itself was found from the accessibility tree), and a barber booking backlog that requires 'Given NVDA on the calendar, then the date, availability and selection are announced' (2026-09-28). The faults they find are the booking ones: names that omit what the sighted user sees, and announced labels that differ from the visible text. Where a release gate asks for a qualified human NVDA reviewer and a signed report (a clinic appointments demo, 2026-11-09), an automated transcript does not close it.
ideas.description: The developer signs in, adds a booking page address (proved by a meta tag or a staging address), and names the labels of its steps: service, staff, time, customer details, confirm, and a deliberate error. A hosted worker built on Screen Reader Journeys runs that journey by keyboard in the walker mode (what Chromium gives a screen reader) and the virtual mode (an emulated screen reader's speech), stopping before the final confirm on a live address. Booking rules read the transcript and focus log and flag the known faults in plain words. For real speech, a GitHub Action runs the same journey under NVDA and Orca in the developer's own repository, comments the diff on the pull request, and adds the transcript to a dated evidence page the developer can share with the client, labelled with the mode or screen reader and version and worded as a record, not an audit.
ideas.targetCustomer: Freelance developers, small agencies and indie teams (1 to 10 people) whose booking flow's code is in their own repository: custom or self-hosted booking pages for local service businesses, and small booking and appointment products. Not sites that embed a hosted booking platform or plugin the developer cannot change (SimplyBook.me, for one, offers its own WCAG 2.1 AA booking theme: https://simplybook.me/en/accessibility).
ideas.buyer: The developer or agency, by card from its tools budget: free for one flow in the hosted modes, $19 a month for one developer with the CI Action and evidence pages, $49 a month for an agency with ten client flows and its own branding; the salon or clinic receives the evidence page and may be billed for it in the build fee.
ideas.whyNow: Since September 2026, small booking and appointment projects, some of them run with coding agents, leave the spoken screen-reader check open while automated checks pass (https://github.com/OpenResilienceInitiative/ORISO-Frontend/issues/2377). The engine that listens is already free: the owner's Screen Reader Journeys, launched 2026-11-25 (https://github.com/pisan-labs/screen-reader-journeys). BrowserStack's screen-reader scans are a public beta on paid plans (https://www.browserstack.com/docs/accessibility/screen-reader-launcher/screen-reader-scan). What is new is a booking-specific check and a record a developer can hand to a client. ADA Title III suits ran at 5,006 in the first half of 2026 (vendor-produced: https://stacker.com/stories/small-business/website-accessibility-lawsuits-are-rising-and-smaller-businesses-are).
ideas.founderFit: He ships a web app alone in days and teaches courses that use agentic coding tools, the way of working whose agents leave this spoken check open; nothing in his stated network reaches booking-page developers.

A reported barrier, found without a screen reader.

Its comments were posted through a coding agent's connector, and the gate asks for a qualified human reviewer with NVDA and Chrome and a dated, signed report, so an automated transcript would not close it.

problemEvidence.summary: Developer of a barbershop's booking app (organisation repository created 2026-09-27, issue opened the next day): a date picker and time-slot story imported from a backlog file, with 'Given NVDA on the calendar, then the date, availability and selection are announced' and, in its business rules, 'Slot toggles use aria-pressed'; still open, with later commits adding Playwright and axe suites and a booking calendar label fix (2026-11-17). A planned acceptance check, not a reported barrier.

A real fault, found by reading code, not by listening; open.

problemEvidence.summary: An NHS design team building appointment booking asks for guidance on selecting one slot from a variable number, including 'screen-reader behaviour'; a contributor replies there is no agreed NHS pattern yet. competitors.price: Unknown: beta, access on request, not on the pricing page; BrowserStack's screen-reader testing starts at Live Team Pro, $249 a month billed annually, and no free plan includes it (https://www.browserstack.com/pricing)

Beta, behind a BrowserStack account, no CI or API stated, no client-facing record.

competitors.price: $19 a month (120 minutes, NVDA and Narrator) or $99 a month (unlimited minutes)

mvpScope.buildEstimate: About 3 weeks as a vertical of Screen Reader Journeys

ideas.techStack: React + Vite front end, Supabase sign-in and per-app schema, the Screen Reader Journeys worker on Render (headless Chromium; walker mode and Guidepup's Virtual Screen Reader), a GitHub Action wrapping Guidepup for NVDA on Windows runners and Orca on Ubuntu runners in the customer's repository, Resend for email, a hosted payment link.

pricing.model: Per-developer and per-agency subscription, with a free hosted tier
pricing.pricePoint: Free for one flow (hosted modes); $19 a month per developer; $49 a month per agency (10 client flows, branded evidence pages)
pricing.rationale: Matches Assistiv Labs' $19 Freelancer plan for manual real-reader minutes (which gives open-source projects free access) and sits far below BrowserStack's $249 and $1,099 plans. The paid tier must earn its price over the free Screen Reader Journeys engine it runs on, so it charges only for the booking rules, the client page and the re-check; the CI minutes are the customer's own.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 60 developers x $19 + 15 agencies x $49 = $1,140 + $735 = $1,875 MRR, assuming about 2% of free hosted users convert and the Marketplace listing brings a steady trickle; unproven.
ideas.distribution: 1) GitHub Marketplace listing of a free composite action that wraps the engine's NVDA and Orca workflows and links to the paid evidence pages: 'The action must be in a public repository', 'Each repository must contain a single action metadata file (action.yml or action.yaml) at the root', the owner accepts the Marketplace Developer Agreement and uses two-factor authentication, and listings that meet the requirements 'are published to GitHub Marketplace immediately and aren't reviewed by GitHub' (https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/actions/how-tos/create-and-publish-actions/publish-in-github-marketplace). 2) A notice inside Screen Reader Journeys for its signed-in users (the owner's own product; no outside rule). 3) Search ads on screen-reader-testing queries: Google Ads rule unknown, check before posting. Not Show HN: 'New features and upgrades ("Foo 1.3.1 is out") generally aren't substantive enough to be Show HNs' and 'Don't post quickly-generated one-offs' (https://news.ycombinator.com/showhn.html), and the engine's own Show HN is drafted for 8 December 2026. Accessibility mailing lists and Slack groups: rule unknown, check before posting. Never in the evidence issues or their repositories.

validationTest.method: Build a demo booking page of the owner's own with five seeded faults and publish a sample evidence page from it. Put both on a landing page that says plainly that the engine is the free Screen Reader Journeys and what the paid tier adds (the booking journey and rules, the dated client page, the weekly re-check), with a free hosted check of the demo, a $19 a month and a $49 a month price button, and a waitlist that asks for the booking page address and whether its code is in the developer's own repository. Drive traffic with a two-week search-ad test on queries such as 'screen reader test booking form' and 'NVDA test my website' (Google Ads rules: check before posting) and a notice to signed-in Screen Reader Journeys users. No outreach to anyone, no Show HN for a landing page, nothing posted in any evidence thread.
validationTest.successCriteria: From about 400 visitors in two weeks: 15 or more price-button clicks, 8 or more waitlist sign-ups whose booking code is in their own repository, and at least 3 paid pre-orders at $19 or more.
validationTest.cost: About 2 days of work and $150 to $250 in search ads.

ideas.moat: Thin: a booking fault library tuned on real flows, each client's history of transcripts, and agencies' branded evidence pages. The engine underneath is the owner's own free MIT tool, and anyone can add booking rules to it.
compliance: ADA Title III and WCAG 2.2 AA: the evidence page records what a named mode or screen reader announced on a date; it is not an audit, makes no conformance claim and is not legal advice.

Live bookings: runs on a live address stop before the final confirm and use synthetic details; full journeys run only on a staging or test-mode address; the developer proves control of the address first.
Health data: clinic flows use synthetic patient details only; no real patient data is entered or stored, so HIPAA is not engaged; say so in the terms.
GDPR: accounts hold an email and run artifacts; screenshots and transcripts have retention caps (Screen Reader Journeys already prunes runs).

GitHub terms (effective 2026-08-27): Actions 'should not be used for' 'The provision of a stand-alone or integrated application or service offering the Actions product or service', for commercial purposes; on GitHub-hosted runners, not for activity unrelated to the software project associated with the repository where Actions are used; and 'You may only access and use GitHub Actions to develop and test your application(s)' (https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-for-additional-products-and-features). Real-reader runs therefore happen in the repository that holds the booking code, never in a HintWise repository on the customer's behalf, and the Action's docs say it checks that repository's own booking flow, not other sites.
Accessibility of the app itself: checked with Screen Reader Journeys before launch.
The evidence page is not the signed human screen-reader review some release gates require, and says so.

risks.risk: BrowserStack's beta screen-reader automation and its plain-words Experience Agent move down-market and cover the booking case.
risks.mitigation: Stay priced for freelancers, keep the booking rules and the client page as the product, and run in the developer's own CI at no runner cost to HintWise.

risks.risk: The signal is inflated: many issues are checklists written by coding agents, and the projects are tiny, so few will pay.
risks.mitigation: Run the price-button test before building; count Marketplace installs, not issues.

risks.risk: One booking journey does not fit the variety of booking interfaces, and per-site fixes turn it into a service.
risks.mitigation: Journeys are named steps over roles and accessible names that the developer edits; no custom work is sold.

risks.risk: Real NVDA and Orca runs are flaky on CI runners.
risks.mitigation: Retry once, compare with the virtual mode, and mark a run inconclusive rather than failed.

risks.risk: A client treats the evidence page as proof of compliance in a dispute.
risks.mitigation: Plain wording on every page: a dated record of what was heard, not an audit or legal advice.

risks.risk: Salons on hosted booking platforms cannot fix a third-party widget, so the salon is not a buyer.
risks.mitigation: Sell to the developers who own the booking code; leave hosted-platform widgets out of scope.

risks.risk: The paid vertical competes with the owner's own free engine: a developer can write the booking journey as a journey file and run it in the free NVDA and Orca workflows.
risks.mitigation: Charge only for what the free engine lacks (booking rules, client page, scheduled re-check) and say on the page that the engine is free.

scoreRationale.pain: Of six organisation-owned items, only one is a human-reported barrier, found from the accessibility tree (https://github.com/OpenResilienceInitiative/ORISO-Frontend/issues/2377); the others are a bot-filed fault (https://github.com/Paige-Agent-AI/Paige-Agent-AI/issues/1480), an agent-commented gate on a synthetic demo that wants a human reviewer (https://github.com/ARG-Digital-Solutions/aronexa-qa-central/issues/4), a backlog import, a design question and a student task, and none comes from the named customer: 2.
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: Freelancers pay $19 a month for manual real-reader minutes, though open-source projects get them free (https://assistivlabs.com/pricing), and screen-reader testing at BrowserStack starts at $249 a month billed annually (https://www.browserstack.com/pricing); nobody in the evidence pays, and the engine is free: 3, the gate's minimum.
scoreRationale.reachability: The buyers are outside the owner's stated network; Show HN rules out feature upgrades and the engine's own Show HN is drafted for 8 December (https://news.ycombinator.com/showhn.html), leaving one unproven self-serve channel, the unreviewed Marketplace listing (https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/actions/how-tos/create-and-publish-actions/publish-in-github-marketplace): 2.
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: The owner's free engine already runs role-and-name journeys and real NVDA and Orca in workflows other repositories can call (https://github.com/pisan-labs/screen-reader-journeys), Guidepup is free and widely installed (https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-month/@guidepup/guidepup), and BrowserStack's agent covers four of the five booking rules (https://www.browserstack.com/docs/accessibility/screen-reader-launcher/screen-reader-experience-agent); what is left is a booking journey, two rules, a client record and a re-check: 1.
scoreRationale.feasibility: The engine and its CI workflows exist (https://github.com/pisan-labs/screen-reader-journeys), but the hosted worker runs only its own journeys on a capped free plan, user journeys widen the sandbox, one journey must fit many booking interfaces, and Actions are 'to develop and test your application(s)' only (https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-for-additional-products-and-features); about 3 weeks of work: 3.
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Wording as a dated record, not an audit (https://stacker.com/stories/small-business/website-accessibility-lawsuits-are-rising-and-smaller-businesses-are); the page must never stand in for the signed human review that gates ask for (https://github.com/ARG-Digital-Solutions/aronexa-qa-central/issues/4); plus the stop-before-confirm guard and the GitHub terms: 4.

review.findings: The reviewer read all six cited issues, each in an organisation-owned repository and dated 2026-09-26 to 2026-11-19. Only one is a human-reported barrier, an appointment calendar whose button names leave out the modality, found from Chromium's accessibility tree without a screen reader; the rest are a fault filed by a bot account, an agent-commented gate on a synthetic demo that asks for a qualified human NVDA reviewer and a signed report (so an automated transcript would not close it), a backlog import, an NHS design question and a student-programme task, and none comes from a freelancer building for a local business, so pain drops from 3 to 2. No free tool does the whole job, but the owner's own free Screen Reader Journeys already runs role-and-name journeys in walker and virtual modes and real NVDA and Orca in workflows other repositories can call, Guidepup (MIT, about 978,000 npm downloads in the month to 2026-11-26) covers developers who write tests, a free Action runs AI-driven NVDA tests on pull requests, and BrowserStack's paid beta agent already checks unique names, feedback after an action, dialog focus and form error announcements under real NVDA, so competitiveGap drops from 2 to 1, re-scoped to a ready booking journey, the selected-slot and silent-availability rules, a dated client record and a scheduled re-check, for developers who own their booking code. Show HN's rules say feature upgrades generally do not qualify and the engine's own Show HN is drafted for 8 December, leaving the unreviewed Marketplace listing as the one self-serve channel, so reachability drops from 3 to 2. The GitHub terms reading holds, and the terms add that Actions may be used only to develop and test your own application, so the CI path fits only repositories that hold the booking code; the total is 15 and it ships as a provisional wildcard.

ideas.wildcardReason: It is the small-business vertical of Screen Reader Journeys, the project that most excited the owner, and adds what its free engine lacks: a booking journey, booking fault rules, and a dated record a developer can hand to a client. It fits testing with assistive technology and tools for working with coding agents.

runNotes.caveats: First run of 2026-11-27 (Friday, customer-facing small-business lens; focus sources A13 with community.shopify.com, B11 and C8). Four regular ideas ship, all provisional (Bill Leak Check 20, Holiday Pre-Order Page 19, Blind Cash Close 19, Menu and Specials Desk 17), and a provisional wildcard (Spoken Booking Check, 15); none came near the gate of 22. Twenty-four candidates were generated (22 with a small-business buyer, 4 aimed at the owner's interests) plus the one watchlist entry, Checker Second Opinion, which was re-researched, fell to 18 and left the watchlist. Six were researched (none ended in research) and six reviewed: five regular reviews, of which one was killed (Walk-In Review Ask, free tools cover it) and four survived as rescores (Bill Leak 20 unchanged in total, Holiday Pre-Order 21 to 19, Blind Cash Close 21 to 19, Menu and Specials Desk 21 to 17), and one wildcard review (18 to 15). Three ideas had survived after five regular reviews, so the review target was met. Selection constraints: every idea has a small-business buyer; ideas 1 to 4 are substantial Multi-week ideas with build plans; at most two share a category (ideas 1 and 3 Small Business Ops, ideas 2 and 4 Micro-SaaS with smallBusiness true, the wildcard Accessibility & Compliance). The constraint of at least one Weekend MVP cannot be met: every surviving idea needs a platform connection (Shopify, Square or Google) and a scheduled job, and Bill Leak Check's CSV-only core would be a Weekend MVP but cannot list on the Shopify App Store without the app shell. Ideas 2 and 3 both serve Square food and cash counters but solve different problems (pre-orders and the cash close); idea 4 shares its customer with the published Fee Disclosure Check for Restaurants (2026-11-06) and State-Code Food Safety Logs (2026-11-13) but not their problem. The wildcard is a vertical of the owner's own Screen Reader Journeys, and its reviewer found the free engine already does much of the job, so it should be weighed as a module of that project, not a new app. Square's App Marketplace has paused new listings and its community forbids unprompted promotion, so ideas 2 and 3 rely on search ads alone; Google Business Profile API access (idea 4) was reported stalled for weeks in 2026 developer threads. Holiday Pre-Order Page cannot be built in time for Christmas 2026; its test runs now and the build targets the Valentine's Day to Easter seasons.
